"API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.prompt:
Search this repository very thoroughly for any per-user API rate-limiting middleware. Look for:
1. Any files referencing "rate limit", "rateLimit", "rate_limit", "throttle", "throttling"
2. Any middleware registration that enforces request limits per user
3. Any configuration of request limits (e.g., requests per minute/hour/second)

Search broadly across the entire codebase — grep for these terms, check middleware directories, check server setup files, API route files, etc. Report what you find, including file paths and line numbers.

content.text:
Based on my thorough search of the entire repository, here are my findings:

---

**This codebase has NO per-user API rate-limiting middleware.** There is no mechanism anywhere in the repository that tracks, counts, or throttles API requests on a per-user basis.

Here is a detailed breakdown of what I searched and what I found:

### 1. Direct term searches

- **"rate limit" / "rateLimit" / "rate_limit"**: Only found in two places, both in the email package as documentation/examples, not actual implementations:
  - `/bench/repo/internal/email/doc.go` line 86 -- a comment suggesting "Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse" (no implementation)
  - `/bench/repo/internal/email/README.md` lines 286-297 -- a documentation example showing how one *could* use `golang.org/x/time/rate` for email sending (not actual code, just a Markdown code block in a README)

- **"throttle" / "throttling"**: No results anywhere in the codebase.

### 2. Rate limiting libraries

- **Go dependencies** (`go.mod` / `go.sum`): No rate limiting libraries are imported. Specifically, none of these are present: `golang.org/x/time/rate`, `httprate`, `tollbooth`, `ulule/limiter`, `throttled`, or any similar package.
- **JavaScript/TypeScript dependencies**: No rate limiting npm packages (e.g., `express-rate-limit`, `rate-limiter-flexible`, `bottleneck`, `p-throttle`) are present.

### 3. Middleware registration

The server at `/bench/repo/server/server.go` registers only two middleware functions (lines 51-52):
- `middleware.Recover()` -- panic recovery
- `newCORSMiddleware(profile)` -- CORS handling

The Connect RPC interceptor chain at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` lines 133-137 registers four interceptors:
- `MetadataInterceptor` -- converts HTTP headers to gRPC metadata
- `LoggingInterceptor` -- logs requests
- `RecoveryInterceptor` -- recovers from panics
- `AuthInterceptor` -- authentication/authorization

None of these implement any form of rate limiting or throttling.

### 4. Related but distinct limiting mechanisms found

The codebase does have some non-rate-limiting resource controls:

- **Request body size limit**: `maxAPIRequestBytes = 256 << 20` (256 MiB) at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` line 20. This limits payload size, not request frequency.
- **Concurrency semaphores**: Thumbnail generation is limited to 3 concurrent operations and image processing to 2 concurrent operations via `golang.org/x/sync/semaphore` at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` lines 59-60 and `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` line 116. These limit concurrent processing, not per-user request rates.
- **Page size cap**: `MaxPageSize = 1000` at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/common.go` line 17. This limits result set sizes, not request frequency.
- **Content length limit**: `getContentLengthLimit` in `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go` line 595 limits memo content length.
- **`codes.ResourceExhausted`**: Used at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/attachment_service.go` line 160 when the image processing semaphore cannot be acquired -- this is a concurrency limit, not a per-user rate limit.

### 5. HTTP 429 / Rate limit headers

No occurrences of HTTP status code 429 (`StatusTooManyRequests`), `Retry-After` headers, or `X-RateLimit-*` headers exist anywhere in the codebase.

### 6. Login attempt limiting

No brute-force protection or login attempt throttling exists. The authentication session code at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/auth_service_session.go` line 277 has only a comment mentioning "Identify suspicious login attempts" but no implementation.

### Summary

This repository (usememos/memos) does not implement any per-user API rate-limiting middleware. There are no request-frequency limits of any kind -- no token buckets, sliding windows, fixed windows, or any other rate limiting algorithms. The only resource controls present are concurrency semaphores for CPU-intensive operations and payload size limits, neither of which qualifies as per-user rate limiting.
